title: POW02: Power, Four Ways: How to Stop Treating Influence Like a Dirty Word
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Claydon argues that leaders default to power over and should instead choose deliberately among four meanings of power: over, with, to and through. Opening with a meeting whose decision was already made, he gives each mode its origin, where it helps, its failure mode and an upgrade move, drawing on Taylor, Follett, Weber and Parsons and network research. The practical thrust is to keep power over as an emergency brake while designing the environment so that with, to and through dominate. He adds a short exercise, common traps and a single action for the week: pre-publish an agenda with the decision, criteria and options plus a dissent slot. The aim is to make influence a deliberate, honest tool rather than a dirty word.
points: Power over is useful in emergencies but corrosive as the only move, producing fear and consultation theatre.
Power with shares the frame, meaning the decision and criteria, not just the floor, and still ends in a decision.
Power to builds light structures such as decision logs and shared playbooks, but risks bureaucracy if rituals are never pruned.
Power through spreads influence via relationships and must avoid dependence on one hero connector.
A pre-published agenda with criteria, two options and a dissent slot moves a team from over to with in one step.
quotes: We inherit power over as default—someone above tells someone below what to do. Useful sometimes; corrosive when it’s the only move.
If you must use over, make it transparent, contestable, proportionate, purpose-linked. Say why, time-box it, invite one round of dissent, and log the decision.
Share the frame not just the floor: publish the decision to be made and the criteria first. Rotate who chairs, not who speaks. Keep a dissent slot, then decide.
Weber analysed how authority is legitimated and routinised; Parsons reframed power as a generalized medium—organisational capacity to mobilise resources toward collective goals.
Bottom line: Power isn’t a dirty word—it’s a vocabulary. Speak with, to, and through by design. Keep over visible and rare. The room will get smarter, faster, and fairer—and so will your leadership.
Design your week so with / to / through do the heavy lifting. Keep over as the emergency brake, not the driving style.
None of these are moral categories. They’re tools. The art is choosing the right one, then building the environment where the better tools win by default.
